text: Mostly because admitting you were wrong feels uncomfortable, especially in front of others. People also tend to look for information that supports what they already believe and ignore the rest. I don't think changing your mind is weak at all; it usually means you've listened and thought carefully. Refusing to change even when the facts are clear is much more worrying.

text: It can. Apps show us content similar to what we've already liked, so it's easy to end up surrounded by people who think exactly like us. Over time, other views start to seem strange or even hostile. The solution isn't to leave social media, but to follow a few sources you disagree with and to talk to real people outside your usual circle.

text: In the end, yes, because they're the ones who will live with the consequences. But at seventeen it's hard to know what a job is really like, so advice from parents and people working in that field is very valuable. I think parents should share their experience and point out risks, but not make the final choice, because people rarely succeed in a career they didn't choose.

text: It really depends on what's at stake. For small things, like what to eat or which film to watch, spending a long time deciding is a waste of energy. For big choices, like moving city or changing jobs, it's worth waiting a few days and collecting information. The risk with taking too long, though, is that good opportunities sometimes disappear while you're still thinking.

text: Definitely. When a manager admits a mistake, it shows the team that it's safe to be honest, so problems are reported earlier instead of being hidden. Some people think it looks weak, but in my experience employees respect a boss who says, 'I got that wrong, let's fix it,' much more than one who blames everyone else.
